Comment on “Influence of Solvents and Halogenation on ESIPT of
Benzimidazole Derivatives for Designing Turn-on Fluorescence
Probes”
Daniela Nedeltcheva-Antonova and Liudmil Antonov*
Cite This: ACS Omega 2025, 10, 22297−22301 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: In the paper, listed in the title, unproper conformation analysis of a series of potentially tautomeric benzimidazole
derivatives has been performed by Rivelino, Canuto, and coauthors (ACS Omega 2024, 9 (20), 22102). They described existence of
only 3 conformers of the enol tautomer and one for the keto form for each of the studied compounds. Actually, we found more than
50 additional conformers for the tautomers of the unsubstituted compound (H). When one bears in mind the structural similarity
with the rest of the compounds, the situation with them should be the same. More importantly, Rivelino, Canuto, and coauthors
discuss in detail the properties of the conformers that are not the most stable ones, which strongly limits the practical value of the
published massive data output. Due to the improperly done theoretical work along with the lack of understanding of the existing
experimental data and principles of excited state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT), the suggested photocycle in the Br
substituted compound (Br) is doubtful.
1. CONFORMATIONAL ANALYSIS
In their paper, Rivelino, Canuto and coauthors1 base the
conformational analysis on the dihedral angles ϕ and ψ (Figure
1), which are responsible for the twisting of the benzimidazole
ring around the C7−C8 bond and rotation of the nonconjugated phenyl ring around the C14−C15 single bond.
When one bears in mind that the nonconjugated phenyl ring is
attached to the rest of the molecule by a CH2 spacer, the
flexibility is driven also by the rotation around the N1−C14
single bond. In addition, the position of both OH groups must
be taken into account along with angle η, describing the steric

hindrance of the conjugated phenyl ring and the CH2 group.
The conformational analysis was performed again in n-hexane
by using the Gaussian 16 C.01 program suite2 using the level of
theory of Rivelino, Canuto, and coauthors (B3LYP3/6-
31G(d,p) level of theory), and the results were additionally
confirmed by using M06-2X4,5/TZVP6, which is more suitable
for tautomeric compounds and their E/Z isomerization in the
ground state.7−10 All structures were optimized without
restrictions using tight optimization criteria and an ultrafine
grid in the computation of two-electron integrals and their
derivatives. The true minima were verified by performing
frequency calculations in the corresponding environment. The
implicit solvation was described using the Polarizable
Continuum Model11 (the integral equation formalism variant,
IEFPCM, as implemented in Gaussian 16).
The structural information and relative energies of the
conformers of the enol and keto tautomers of H are collected
in Table S1. As is seen, the enol conformers III and II, stated
by Rivelino, Canuto and coauthors, are not the most stable
ones and represent E2 and E5 in the Table S1. The conformer
V corresponds to K8, which again is not the most stable keto
conformer. As seen from Figure 2, substantial stabilization is

achieved by formation of intramolecular C�O···H−O hydrogen bonding. To prove that the energy stabilization of E1 is
meaningful, additionally, M06-2X/TZVP optimization was
done, showing that, in the paper listed in the title, the
conformational analysis is wrong. This fact makes the
information, listed in Tables 1−5 in the text of Rivelino,
Canuto, and coauthors, and the overall discussion and
conclusions about the conformational analysis of the whole
series of compounds ill-based.
2. EXCITED STATE INTRAMOLECULAR PROTON
TRANSFER PHOTOCYCLE IN Br
Bearing in mind the availability of previous spectral data for Br
in a variety of solvents,12 Rivelino, Canuto, and coauthors
aimed to consider in depth the mechanism of the excited state
intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT). As already mentioned
above, they base the theoretical model on E2, which is not the
most stable structure in the ground state, but this is not the
major problem. In Figure 7 in their text, a scheme of the
suggested ESIPT model is shown. However, the studied
benzimidazoles, where twisting around the C7−C8 bond is
possible (flexible ESIPT skeleton13,14), have a more
complicated overall ESIPT mechanism. In its general form, it
can be illustrated with the case of 1-methyl-2-(2′-
hydroxyphenyl)benzimidazole (NMeHPBI, N1-CH3 analog
of H), which has been studied in depth by variety of
experimental techniques15−17 and theoretical modeling.18−21
The schematic presentation of ESIPT and the related
processes is sketched in Figure 3. The enol form, only existing
in the ground state, upon excitation can either relax back (local
enol emission) to the ground state or exhibit a very fast ESIPT,
giving the excited KE tautomer (cis-keto considering the
mutual position of the proton exchanging O and N atoms),
where intramolecular hydrogen bonding exists. In its turn, it

can return (ESIPT emission) to the virtual ground state KE
tautomer, which by barrierless ground state intramolecular PT
(GSIPT) restores the initial E or through twisting motion
reaches the conical intersection region, where the phenyl and
benzimidazolyl rings are essentially perpendicular to each other
and populate simultaneously both KE and the trans-keto KK
(which then relaxes to E thermally). The latter process is the
major emissionless deactivation channel. It is stronger in the
N-R substituted benzimidazoles (such as NMeHPBI or
NEtHPBI22,23) compared to the structurally similar, but
planar, 2-(2′-hydroxyphenyl)benzoxazole24 and 2-(2′-
hydroxyphenyl)benzothiazole,25,26 because the steric hindrance between R and the phenyl ring reduces planarity and
pushes the molecule in the excited state twisting region. As a
result, the emission spectra of NMeHPBI in non-polar aprotic
solvents consists of two bands: one in the range of 350−400
nm, attributed to the local emission of the enol form, and
second, the typical ESIPT emission, strongly red shifted in the
range of 400−500 nm (with a Stokes shift of 11 000 cm−1 in
cyclohexane and 1,4-dioxane15). [The exact situation depends
on the solvent. In cycloxehane, only the ESIPT emission is
detected at 496 nm with quantum yield between 9%15 and
4%17. In 1,4-dioxane, the local enol emission is detected at 351
nm (quantum yield of 40%) and ESIPT emission is measured
at 495 nm (quantum yield of 5%15). In methanol, according to
Shida and co-workers17 only local enol emits at 353 nm
(quantum yield of 30%), while according to Douhal at al.15
both local (349 nm, quantum yield of 38%) and ESIPT (472
nm, quantum yield of 25) are detected. In methanol, the
absorption spectrum has, in addition to the main peak at 330

nm, an additional broad absorption in the range of 340−370
nm, and the excitation at 360 nm gives an emission at 423 nm.
The situation in acetonitrile and ethanol is similar.16] Upon
addition of water or alcohols, as a result of partial or full
breakage of the intramolecules and formation of intermolecular
solute-solvent hydrogen bonding, the ESIPT emission
becomes less intense or disappears.15−17
The comparison between Figure 3 here and Figure 7 in the
work of Rivelino, Canuto, and coauthors shows very clearly
why the latter is wrong. The ESIPT process occurs through

hydrogen bonding and results in KE*, a structure where this
hydrogen bonding still exists. The correct structures can be
seen in Figure 4 and, in detail, in Table S2. The ground state
keto form V, shown in Figure 7, produced by Rivelino, Canuto
and coauthors,1 can be obtained only after twisting and can be
populated only through conical intersection from the excited
state. It represents the KK form (K8) but not the most stable
one (K1), which is stabilized by OH···O�C hydrogen
bonding, as shown in Table S2. The shown excited state
keto tautomer IV cannot be obtained by a ESIPT process from

III (Figure 6 in ref 1). In this way, Figure 7 in the work of
Rivelino, Canuto and coauthors does not show the ESIPT
process.
It is worth noting that the photophysical cycle in Br is rather
complicated due to the flexibility around the spacer (C14). As
a result, an ensemble of enol forms with very near energies
exists in the ground state (E1−E6), easily converted to each
other. Upon excitation, some of them are giving excited state
enols; in some, the ESIPT is direct to the keto form, as seen in
Tables S2 and S3. Upon twisting of the formed KE*, the
flexibility in the N-R part leads to a formation of OH···O�C
in the conical intersection region relaxing finally to KK (K1).
The obtained K1 easily coverts back to the enol ensemble
through series of steps involving K2 and K4 (depending on the
direction of twisting motion). This means that KK cannot be
trapped, and consequently, an emission coming from it could
not be seen. Following the discussion, two possible emissions
could be expected: the local emission of the enol and the low
intensive (due to the formation of the OH···O�C bond, the
twisting should be preferred) emission coming from the return
of KE* to the ground state. However, the studied compound
has a unique structure allowing an additional OH···N
intramolecular hydrogen bonding, namely, O2−H6···N1 (see
structure E4, Tables S2 and S3). Potentially, upon excitation of
the existing traces of E4 (see Table S2), an additional ESIPT
could be expected in this moiety, giving zwitterionic KE4′*,
which then relaxes directly to E4, giving as an option very weak
emission blue shifted with respect to the local emission of E4.
Probability for this ESIPT process is low but potentially exits if
a ballistic PT is considered from the enol Frank-Condon state.
In other words, Br could exhibit a triple emission coming
(from blue to red) from KE4′*, E*, and KE*.
What do the experimental data for Br show? According to

the absorption and NMR spectra of Br, no sights of the keto
tautomer in the ground state are seen. This is an expected
result coming from the fact that the transition from enol to
keto reduces the aromatic character of the phenyl ring.
According to the published emission spectra of Br, the
following emission is detected in low polar aprotic solvents (nhexane, 1,4-dioxane, toluene, and benzene) and in chloroform:
a weak band at 330 nm, slightly depending on the solvents, a
more intensive band in the range of 340−350 nm, and a broad
and weak shoulder after 370 nm (unfortunately, the spectra are
recorded until 380 nm in most of the cases). The addition of
water (in 1,4-dioxane) or change of the solvent to a more polar
one (acetonitrile, DMSO) or protic one (various alcohols)
leads to disappearance of the blue shifted emission, but in most
of the cases, the broad shoulder after 370 nm remains. The
emission around 350 nm is attributed, based on using model
compounds, to the local emission of the enol tautomer.
Erroneously, the disappearance of the blue shifted emission is
attributed to breakage of the intramolecular hydrogen bonding
between O1 and N2 making the ESIPT process impossible. As
proven above, the ESIPT process between O1 and N2 is
attributed to the red shifted emission with large Stokes shifts,
with respect to the local emission of the enol. The Stokes shifts
for Br in n-hexane, calculated from ref 12, are correspondingly
3300 and 4800 cm−1
, so if one assumes that the first band
comes from ESIPT between O1 and N2, it should be either
coming from high energy excited keto tautomer or assigned to
a lower, compared to the enol, energy ground state. In the first
case, ESIPT between O1 and N2 is impossible (ESIPT from
low energy E* to high energy KE*) and in the second, the
ground state keto form, being more stable than the enol,
should be seen in the absorption spectra, which is not the case.

However, when one takes into account the additional
possibility for ESIPT between O2 and N1, as shown by the
theory above, a reasonable explanation is the blue shifted
emission comes from the excited state zwitterionic form. When
one bears in mind that the hydrogen bonding between O2 and
N1 is weaker compared to that between O1 and N2, the
former should be more easily broken by water or alcohols,
which exactly happens. Of course, here, we give a very
simplified explanation of a very complex photophysical cycle
and detailed experimental studies are needed to shed more
light on reality.
To conclude, in order to adequately model a given process,
one must go deeply into the problem to understand the details,
to acknowledge the possible pitfalls, and critically to study the
existing experimental data. This was not done in the paper we
discuss. The conformational analysis is not performed
properly, which reduces the applicability of the presented
massive theoretical output. The suggested model of the ESIPT
in Br neglects the basic principles of this process and actually
does not represent a real ESIPT.
